Unit 8 💰 Commercialization

Pricing & Packaging in the Agent Era

⏱️ 25 minutes • 📖 Reading + Examples

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Understand the evolution from seat-based to consumption-based to outcome-based pricing
  • Learn how SAP's Capacity Unit model works for HANA Cloud and Datasphere
  • Recognize the PMM's role in pricing strategy and value communication
  • Apply pricing principles to data platform and AI product positioning

The Pricing Tectonic Shift

For decades, enterprise software pricing followed a simple formula: count the humans, multiply by a price. Named users. Concurrent users. Seats. The model was predictable, easy to budget, and aligned with how companies thought about software adoption.

Then three forces converged to break it:

  1. Cloud infrastructure made compute and storage variable costs, not fixed assets
  2. API-first architectures meant software increasingly talked to other software, not humans
  3. AI agents began doing work that humans used to do—but don't need "seats"

The result? According to Metronome's 2025 State of Usage-Based Pricing report, 77% of the largest software companies now incorporate consumption-based pricing into their revenue models. And it's accelerating.

👤
Seat-Based

Per user, per month

📊

💡 Why This Matters for PMM

Pricing isn't just a finance or product decision—it's a positioning decision. How you price signals what you value, who you're for, and how you expect customers to measure success. As PMMs, we own the narrative that makes pricing make sense.

Stage 1: Seat-Based Pricing

The traditional model still dominates legacy enterprise software. It's simple: 10 users = 10 licenses.

Advantages

  • Predictable revenue for the vendor
  • Predictable costs for the buyer (easy to budget)
  • Easy to administer (count heads, bill accordingly)

The Breaking Point

  • Shelfware problem: Companies buy 100 seats, only 40 people use it
  • Adoption misalignment: Vendor gets paid whether customer gets value or not
  • AI disruption: When an agent does the work of 5 analysts, do you need 5 seats?

📌 The CIO.com Warning (November 2025)

"Fueled by workforce reductions, which are in turn driven by AI, vendors are abandoning per-seat pricing and moving to charging by consumption and/or agent interactions."

This shift is forcing CIOs to completely rethink negotiation tactics. Fixed annual contracts are giving way to variable consumption commitments with usage floors and ceilings.

Stage 2: Consumption-Based Pricing

Also called usage-based pricing (UBP), this model charges based on actual consumption—compute cycles, storage gigabytes, API calls, data processed, or custom "units" that represent workload.

The SAP Approach: Capacity Units

SAP has adopted a Capacity Unit (CU) model for its data and analytics portfolio. This is particularly relevant for HANA Cloud, Datasphere, and the broader Business Data Cloud.

🟢 SAP Datasphere Pricing Model (Public)

SAP Datasphere uses Business Technology Platform Capacity Units rather than per-user licensing. According to SAP's public pricing documentation:

  • Flexible allocation: CUs can be applied to compute, storage, or data services
  • Hyperscaler agnostic: Same CU model works across AWS, Azure, and GCP
  • Workload-based: The number of CUs required depends on your specific workload, not user count
  • Adaptable: Scale up or down as data volumes and processing needs change

Understanding Capacity Units

What a CU actually represents

A Capacity Unit is SAP's universal currency for cloud workloads. Think of it like buying "compute credits" that can be spent on different services:

Service CU Consumption Driver
SAP HANA Cloud Memory size × hours running
SAP Datasphere Data storage + compute for modeling
SAP Analytics Cloud Query processing + user activity
Data Integration Volume of data moved/transformed

Benefits of Consumption Pricing

✅ For Customers

  • Pay only for actual usage
  • Scale costs with business value
  • No shelfware waste
  • Lower barrier to start

✅ For Vendors

  • Revenue grows with adoption
  • Natural expansion motion
  • Incentive to drive usage
  • Usage data informs product

The Challenges

⚠️ Bill Shock: The Consumption Pricing Risk

A recent E3 Magazine analysis warned about "cloud bill shock"—when customers see unexpectedly high invoices due to usage spikes they didn't anticipate.

This is why SAP (and most enterprise vendors) offer committed capacity options: buy a block of CUs upfront at a discount, with flexibility to use them across services. It combines the predictability of fixed pricing with the flexibility of consumption.

Stage 3: Outcome-Based Pricing

The frontier of pricing innovation: charge based on the results the software delivers, not the resources it consumes.

This is nascent but growing fast. Gartner predicts that by 2026, 60% of large IT services contracts will include "AI clawback" clauses or outcome-linked levers.

Early Examples

  • Zendesk (August 2024): First major SaaS vendor to launch outcome-based pricing for AI agents—billing per "Automated Resolution" (a support ticket resolved by AI without human intervention)
  • Salesforce Agentforce: Per-conversation pricing model that charges for agent interactions rather than human seats
  • Sierra AI: "We're only paid when we drive real results"—pure outcome-based model

💡 The Measurement Challenge

Outcome-based pricing sounds ideal but is hard to implement. Real business outcomes (revenue increase, cost savings, retention) have multiple inputs. If an AI tool contributes to an outcome but the customer's team or other tools also play a role, how do you attribute success? This complexity is why only ~17% of enterprise SaaS vendors have implemented true outcome-based pricing.

What Outcome-Based Could Look Like for Data Platforms

For SAP's data portfolio, outcome-based pricing might eventually include:

  • Per insight delivered: Charge when an AI-generated insight is viewed/acted upon
  • Per decision supported: Track when data from the platform influences a documented business decision
  • Per automation completed: When data pipelines successfully execute end-to-end workflows
  • Per prediction accuracy: Tie pricing to the accuracy/value of AI model outputs

📌 The Hybrid Reality (2025-2026)

According to Flexera's research, most enterprises are landing on hybrid models: a fixed base subscription with variable consumption add-ons. Pure usage or pure outcome models remain rare because neither vendors nor buyers are ready for the unpredictability.

This is where SAP's BTP Capacity Unit model sits—committed capacity (predictable base) with flexible allocation (consumption flexibility).

The PMM's Role in Pricing

Product marketers don't set prices—but we set the context that makes prices make sense. Here's how pricing intersects with PMM work:

1. Value Articulation

If the price is based on Capacity Units, we need to help customers understand what they get for a CU. Abstract units need concrete value translation.

💡 The Value Bridge

Don't sell "Capacity Units." Sell what CUs enable: "Process 10 million transactions per month" or "Support 500 concurrent analytics users" or "Store 3 years of transactional history with instant query response."

2. Competitive Positioning

Different pricing models create different competitive narratives:

Pricing Model Competitive Angle
Per-seat "Predictable, easy to budget"
Consumption "Pay only for value received"
Outcome "We're so confident we tie our fee to your success"

3. Sales Enablement

Sales teams need to defend pricing in negotiations. PMMs provide:

  • ROI calculators that translate units to business value
  • TCO comparisons showing how consumption models beat alternatives
  • Reference stories of customers who scaled efficiently
  • Objection handlers for "bill shock" and unpredictability concerns

4. Packaging Strategy

How you bundle features affects perceived value. For SAP BDC, this might mean:

  • Starter packages: Fixed CU allocation for predictable entry
  • Growth packages: Committed capacity + burst allowance
  • Enterprise packages: Unlimited within a band, true consumption above

SAP's Pricing Evolution in Context

SAP has been on its own pricing transformation journey:

The RISE with SAP Model

RISE with SAP represents SAP's move toward bundled cloud subscriptions:

  • S/4HANA Cloud as the core
  • BTP credits included for extension and integration
  • Success services bundled in
  • Hyperscaler infrastructure wrapped

This is a hybrid model: fixed subscription base with consumption flexibility for BTP services.

The BDC Opportunity

For the Business Data Cloud team specifically, the Capacity Unit model positions SAP well for the AI era:

  • Workload-based: Pricing reflects actual data processing, not arbitrary user counts
  • AI-ready: When AI agents query HANA Cloud, they consume CUs—no "seat" awkwardness
  • Scalable: Customers can start small and grow consumption as they derive value
  • Unified: Same CU currency across HANA, Datasphere, and Analytics Cloud

🟢 Positioning the CU Model

Old narrative: "How many named users do you need for HANA?"

New narrative: "How much data do you want to activate, and how fast do you need answers?"

The shift from counting people to measuring workload is the foundation for outcome-based pricing evolution.

Looking Ahead: Pricing in the Agentic Era

As AI agents become more prevalent, pricing models will continue evolving:

Near-Term (2026-2027)

  • Hybrid dominates: Fixed base + consumption add-ons remain the norm
  • Agent-specific pricing: New SKUs for AI agent workloads vs. human workloads
  • Committed capacity: Enterprises lock in CU commitments to manage costs

Medium-Term (2027-2028)

  • Outcome experiments: Early adopters pilot outcome-linked pricing for specific use cases
  • Value attribution: Better tools to measure software's contribution to business results
  • Risk sharing: Vendors take on more risk with performance guarantees

Long-Term Vision

  • True outcome-based: "Pay when the AI generates a validated insight that drives action"
  • Autonomous procurement: AI agents comparing pricing models on behalf of buyers
  • Dynamic pricing: Real-time price adjustments based on demand and value delivered

💡 The PMM Opportunity

As pricing becomes more complex, the need for clear value narratives increases. The PMM who can translate abstract units and outcome metrics into compelling business stories will be invaluable.

Key Takeaways

  1. Pricing is evolving from seats → consumption → outcomes, driven by cloud economics and AI
  2. SAP's Capacity Unit model is a consumption-based approach that positions well for AI workloads
  3. Hybrid models dominate because pure consumption or outcome pricing is still too unpredictable
  4. PMMs own the value narrative that makes pricing make sense to buyers
  5. The future is outcome-linked, but measurement and attribution challenges remain
